power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Purpose: We investigated the mechanisms behind the generation of Neural Distortion Responses (NDRs) measured with electroencephalography when interleaving amplitudemodulated (AM) pulse trains in cochlear implant (CI) users.
Methods: Previous experiments measured NDRs using interleaved pulse trains in which oddand even-numbered pulses were respectively modulated at F1 and F2 Hz, where F1=2*F2/3 and F1≈80Hz.
Experiment 1 separated quadratic and cubic distortion products using a relationship of F1 and F2 such that F1 = (2*F2/3)+2.
Experiment 2 retained the original F1=2*F2/3 relationship but shifted the starting AM phase of F2 relative to that of F1.
Experiment 3 simultaneously separated the quadratic and cubic distortion products and varied the relative phase of F1 and F2.
Experiment 4 flipped the leading polarity of the second pulse in each pulse-pair such that the central phase of the resulting pseudo-triphasic pulses was anodic.
All experiments were conducted with Cochlear CI users and interpreted using two computational models of the electrically stimulated auditory nerve.
Results: Both quadratic (QDR) and cubic distortion products (CDR) were observed.
Varying relative AM phase had an effect on NDR amplitudes, with the largest amplitude when maxima of the 2 AM patterns were aligned.
Stimulating with an anodic central phase within the AM pulse pairs resulted in stronger responses for 4 of 9 CI users.
Computational modelling suggested a stronger role for refractoriness than for facilitation in generating the NDR, but failed to fully account for the effect of flipping the polarity.
Conclusion: NDRs consist of both quadratic and cubic components, and are greatest when maxima of the F1 and F2 pulse trains align.
Refractoriness is likely more important than facilitation for generating the NDR.
Cochlear implants (CIs) are neuro-prosthetic devices that have provided a sense of sound to over one million users worldwide by directly stimulating the auditory nerve [1].
text.formatted: Cochlear implants (CIs) are neuro-prosthetic devices that have provided a sense of sound to over one million users worldwide by directly stimulating the auditory nerve <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Although many listeners achieve improved speech-perception using their CI there is a lot of variability between users [2].
text.formatted: Although many listeners achieve improved speech-perception using their CI there is a lot of variability between users <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: This variability has inspired numerous research studies investigating its causes and ways in which CI stimulation can be optimised for improved speech-perception outcomes [3], [4].
text.formatted: This variability has inspired numerous research studies investigating its causes and ways in which CI stimulation can be optimised for improved speech-perception outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: One approach is development of fitting procedures that leverage objective electrophysiological measures reflective of perceptual reports of loudness, with the aim of optimising the stimulation current levels of the CI.

This has been tried primarily using evoked potential recordings from the auditory nerve (electrically evoked compound action potentials, or ECAPs) and brainstem (electrically evoked auditory brainstem responses, or EABRs), with limited and variable correlations with loudness perception [5], [6], [7].
text.formatted: This has been tried primarily using evoked potential recordings from the auditory nerve (electrically evoked compound action potentials, or ECAPs) and brainstem (electrically evoked auditory brainstem responses, or EABRs), with limited and variable correlations with loudness perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: A key limitation of these approaches is that they usually present electrical-current stimulation pulses at a slow rate (< 80 pulses per second, or pps) and measure the responses in the gaps between the stimuli [8].
text.formatted: A key limitation of these approaches is that they usually present electrical-current stimulation pulses at a slow rate (< 80 pulses per second, or pps) and measure the responses in the gaps between the stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: These slow rates are necessary in part to extract the neural response from contamination by the large electrical artefact produced by CI stimulation, but they render the stimulation very different to that used in CI users' every-day 'coding strategies.'

It is therefore desirable to have a technique for measuring neural responses to electrical stimulation in CIs that is as close as possible to those leveraged in everyday use and that isolates these responses from the ubiquitous electrical artefacts.
technique as a way to measure the sustained neural response of CI users to high-rate, amplitude-modulated (AM) pulse trains presented to one or two electrodes in an interleaved manner [9].
text.formatted: technique as a way to measure the sustained neural response of CI users to high-rate, amplitude-modulated (AM) pulse trains presented to one or two electrodes in an interleaved manner <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: The high rate and the amplitude modulation both render the stimulus more similar to stimulation CI users listen to every day, compared to the stimuli used for ECAPs and EABRs.
In ALFIES, two interleaved pulse trains are amplitude-modulated at different frequencies F1 and F2 Hz.
When F1 and F2 were 80 and 120 Hz, respectively, electroencephalography (EEG) recordings revealed the presence of a neural distortion response (NDR) at 40 Hz.

This component is unlikely to reflect nonlinearities in the CI stimulation system because the two AM pulse trains are interleaved in time and nonlinearities from the device occur almost instantaneously.

Conversely, the auditory system responds to each pulse in the stimulation pattern in a way that is not independent of adjacent pulses, via mechanisms that include refractoriness and facilitation at the level of the auditory nerve [10].
text.formatted: Conversely, the auditory system responds to each pulse in the stimulation pattern in a way that is not independent of adjacent pulses, via mechanisms that include refractoriness and facilitation at the level of the auditory nerve <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: This "undoes" the independence of the F1 and F2 pulse trains, allowing subsequent and/or simultaneous nonlinearities within the auditory system to produce NDRs at composite frequencies such as F2-F1.
The NDR had a group delay of approximately 45 milliseconds (ms), consistent with a thalamic and/or cortical neural generator and inconsistent with the zero delay expected from an electrical artefact.

Furthermore, Guérit et al suggested that the temporal integration mechanism that precedes neural nonlinearities to generate an NDR likely occurs as early as the auditory nerve membrane and cochlear nucleus, with these NDRs being propagated to cortical/thalamic generators where they can be detected using EEG [11].
text.formatted: Furthermore, Guérit et al suggested that the temporal integration mechanism that precedes neural nonlinearities to generate an NDR likely occurs as early as the auditory nerve membrane and cochlear nucleus, with these NDRs being propagated to cortical/thalamic generators where they can be detected using EEG <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: This was evidenced by the decrease in NDR amplitude as the inter-pulse interval (IPI) between F1 and F2 pulses . was increased above 200-400 μs, with no measurable response > 900μs [11].

text.text: Thalamic and cortical integration mechanisms would be expected to have longer time constants.
The experiments described here had two broad goals.
The first was to improve our understanding of the neural processes revealed by the ALFIES method.
As noted above, the presence of the NDR demonstrates the operation of some between-pulse temporal dependency or dependencies, followed by one or more nonlinearities.

Understanding the temporal dependencies between pulses is of particular interest given the trend of increasing CI stimulation rates, and hence shorter inter-pulse intervals, in modern CI processing strategies.
Although Guérit et al showed that the dependencies responsible for the NDR had a short time constant reflective of a peripheral basis [11], those data do not distinguish between specific mechanisms.
text.formatted: Although Guérit et al showed that the dependencies responsible for the NDR had a short time constant reflective of a peripheral basis <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, those data do not distinguish between specific mechanisms.

text.text: We therefore use two computational models that, respectively, incorporate facilitation and refractoriness, and evaluate their predictions of the effect of the relative phase of the F1 and F2 modulations on the NDR.
Our experimental results suggest that refractoriness plays the greater role.
We also build on previous ALFIES studies to investigate the nature of the nonlinearity responsible for NDR generation.
The NDR investigated previously could have reflected either a quadratic (F2-F1) and/or a cubic (2*F1-F2) distortion component, as both give rise to distortions at the same frequency when F2 = 1.5*F1.
While these components were intentionally confounded for the purpose of maximising potential SNR, it was not known whether the NDR is quadratic in nature, cubic, or a mixture of both.

In our first experiment, we separated the quadratic (QDR) and cubic distortion responses (CDR) by changing F1 to 82 Hz while keeping F2 at 120 Hz, resulting in separated quadratic and cubic distortion products at 38 and 44 Hz, respectively.
We found both QDRs and CDRs with group delays consistent with thalamo-cortical neural generators.

Given this new evidence that both distortions contribute to the NDR, the importance of optimising parameters such that they interfere constructively became clear, both to maximise SNR and to achieve the most faithful representation of the response of the auditory system.
Experiments 2 to 4 addressed our second motivation, which was to maximise the size of the NDR and to refine the use of ALFIES as a clinical technique.

ALFIES already shows promise in this regard: it measures the sustained response to high-rate pulse-trains while avoiding electrical artefact, requires only a single pair of recording electrodes and standard EEG equipment, has a steep amplitude growth function, and -by presenting the F1 and F2 pulse trains to electrodes separated by varying amounts -has the potential to measure the selectivity as well as sensitivity to CI stimulation [9], [11].
text.formatted: ALFIES already shows promise in this regard: it measures the sustained response to high-rate pulse-trains while avoiding electrical artefact, requires only a single pair of recording electrodes and standard EEG equipment, has a steep amplitude growth function, and -by presenting the F1 and F2 pulse trains to electrodes separated by varying amounts -has the potential to measure the selectivity as well as sensitivity to CI stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: A potential limitation is that the amplitude of the NDR reported in previous studies was lower than that of the electrically evoked steady-state response (eASSR).

We show here that by presenting both the F1 and F2 modulations such that their maxima are aligned, it is possible to produce an NDR amplitude that is comparable to that produced by the eASSR, thereby combining the benefits of the two techniques.
Experiment 4 also shows that the NDR may be further increased for some participants by presenting the F1 and F2 pulses in opposite leading polarity.

All experiments involved direct stimulation of an adjacent pair of electrodes with interleaved, amplitude-modulated pulse trains using the Nucleus Implant Communicator research software version 4.3 (NIC4.3, nice22.1) provided by Cochlear Ltd.

The stimulation parameters were controlled by a laptop using custom software developed in Python version 3.9 (Wilmington, Delaware, USA) that used the NIC4.3 python libraries, and communicated with a CP910 cochlear-implant processor via a programming cable and POD connected to the laptop via USB.
The interleaved AM pulse trains used for stimulation are depicted in Figure 1a-b.

text.text: Each AM pulse train had a carrier rate of 480 pps, usually with a stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA) of 200 μs (except for experiment 4).

These parameters were selected for consistency with previous work and from evidence of no reduction in the NDR amplitude when the AM pulse trains are presented on adjacent electrodes compared to a single electrode, or when the SOA was set to 200-400 μs compared to shorter values [9], [11].

text.text: Some experiments (2, 4) used an F1:F2 ratio of 2:3 as in previous work (see Figure 1a), whereas other experiments (1, 3) added 2 Hz to F1 such that the quadratic and cubic distortion product frequencies were isolated but both still fell within ≈ 40 ± 10 Hz, the optimal range for eliciting a cortical response (see Figure 1b; [12], [13]).

The phase durations and stimulating electrodes differed somewhat across participants (Table 1), with a preference for more-apical electrodes and phase durations that matched those used in the participants' clinical program.

text.text: Longer phase durations were used when compliance limits were reached without achieving a loudness rating of "most-comfortable level" (MCL).
More-basal electrodes were employed when apical electrodes were switched off in the CI user's clinical programme or showed atypically high impedance values.
Prior to commencing, impedances were recorded and the upper limit of compliance was calculated for stimulating electrodes.
A loudness-scaling procedure was then employed using an 11-point chart where0 = 'inaudible' and10 = 'too loud.'

Starting with 0.5-second duration, unmodulated pairs of pulse trains on one electrode that were presented below threshold with slowly increasing current level (with steps of 6 Current Levels or CLs, where 6 CL ≈ 1 dB) until the sounds were just audible.

This level was set as the threshold (T), and then the two interleaved trains were amplitude modulated respectively at 80 and 120 Hz between T and a higher current level that was increased in steps of 6 CLs until level '4' (comfortable but too soft) was achieved, steps of 4 CLs until level '5' (comfortable but soft) was achieved, and steps of 2 CLs until level '7' (loud but comfortable) was achieved.

The upper modulation current level was then decreased in steps of 1 or 2 CLs to find the highest current level that was considered '6' (most comfortable), and this current level was set as MCL for that electrode.
The same procedure was then repeated with the second, adjacent electrode.
These two sets of T and MCL levels were then used as the minimum and maximum current between which the pulse trains were amplitude modulated for the interleaved stimulation.

The participant was played a 5-10 second segment of the interleaved stimulus to confirm that the level was comfortable to listen to for an extended period of time, and the MCL levels were decreased in steps of 2 CLs if necessary to accommodate this.

Research participants were then asked to remove the research processor, and were fit with an electroencephalography (EEG) cap fitted with 10 contacts (including 2 ground electrodes), placed as depicted in Figure 1c.

text.text: The EEG system was custom built by BioSemi B.V. (Amsterdam, Netherlands) with a 262,144 kHz sampling rate.
Stimuli were delivered to the CI via direct stimulation using a CP910 processor in the manner described above, in segments of 31 seconds.

A trigger was included in the stimulation code at each 1-second interval (excluding the first second to avoid onset responses) throughout stimulation, for use in the analysis pipeline that organised the EEG data into 1-second epochs.

The analysis pipeline was employed in real time during data collection as described in Guérit et al (2023) and followed the procedure laid out in both Carlyon et al (2021) and Guérit et al (2023), with some small adjustments described below.

It used custom software developed in MATLAB 2020b (Mathworks, Natick, Massachusetts, USA) that reads in and processes EEG data files saved by the ActiView software (ActiHyper version 804) from Biosemi.

Two phenomenological models of the auditory nerve's response to electrical stimulation were used.

The first model is based on Brochier et al (BR22) and includes spike-rate adaptation and refractoriness [21], while the second is based on Joshi et al (JO17) and also includes facilitation and accommodation [22].

text.text: The simulations showed that at short inter-pulse intervals such as used here, NDR generation was primarily driven by facilitation / summation between the F1 and F2 primaries in the JO17 model, while it was primarily driven by refractoriness / masking in the BR22 model.
The BR22 model consists of 1500 neurons distributed along the cochlea.

For each combination of stimulating electrode and neuron, a look-up table (re-used from Brochier et al.) gives a probability of firing as a function of input current level, based on an inverse cumulative density function of a normal distribution.
The 50-% point of each of these functions was derived in that study using single pulses and a combination of a finite-element method conduction model and a cable model of the auditory nerve.
The relative spread (~slope) of these functions differs from neuron to neuron and matches group statistics from cat auditory nerve recordings.

A stochastic process generates spikes based on such probabilities of firing / look-up table, and if a spike is generated, the input level is elevated to reflect refractoriness and spike-rate adaptation.
Absolute refractoriness lasts 700 μs [24], [25], relative refractoriness is modelled by a 6-dB decreased in input current level going back to 0 dB with a time constant of 1.5 ms.

We created a population-response version of the JO17 model by creating 1500 neurons, matching the single-pulse 50-% firing probabilities of the BR22 model as a function of neuron, stimulating electrode, and level.
The original JO17 model consists of two leaky-integrate-andfire neurons, respectively anodic-and cathodic-sensitive.

Time constants of facilitation (~200 µs), refractoriness (600 µs absolute, up to 4-5 ms relative), accommodation and spike-rate adaptation are not parameters per se, but consequences of the time constants of integration, amounts of leakiness and type of noise in the leaky integrate-and-fire process.
They match single-fibre cat recordings.

For both models, across all experiments and unless otherwise stated, two seconds of interleaved, amplitude-modulated biphasic pulse-train stimuli (designed to replicate the experimental stimuli) were processed with 60 repetitions.
The first second of each segment was ignored to omit any contribution of an onset response and capture only the steady-state output.

The modelled neural responses were then cut in 1-second epochs, averaged, summed across all neurons, and the amplitude and phase at the frequencies of interest were extracted . with an fft with 1-Hz resolution, as was done for the EEG analysis.

To compare the predictions of the two models with the experimental data, three LME models were fit to the NDR amplitudes (in dB re 1 μV) with participant specified as a random factor and an intercept fit for each.
The fitlme() function in MATLAB version 2020b (Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA) was used with the default settings (i.e. the 'FitMethod' was set to 'ML').

The first LME model fit two fixed effects: a cosine and sine curve with periods corresponding to one cycle per π radians of relative AM starting phase of the two interleaved pulse trains (cos2 and sin2, respectively).
This sinusoidal behavior mimics the effect of relative phase estimated by using the BR22 model.

The model structure was: y ~ sin2 + cos2 + (1 + sin2 + cos2 | subj), where y is the NDR amplitude in dB re 1 μV, and sin2 and cos2 are the sinusoid transformations of ϕF2 with periods of π (sin2 = sin(2ϕF2); cos2 = sin(2ϕF2)).
The model's joint test of the two fixed effects was significant (F(2,60) = 12.9773, p < 0.0001), consistent with a significant modulation of the data with a period of π.

This suggests that the highest-amplitude NDRs are observed when the maxima of the AM pulse trains are aligned.

The second LME model fit two fixed effects: a cosine and sine curve with periods corresponding to two cycles per π radians of relative AM starting phase of the two interleaved pulse trains (cos4 and sin4, respectively).
This sinusoidal behaviour mimics the effect of relative phase estimated by using the JO17 model.
The model structure was: y ~ sin4 + cos4 + (1 + sin4 + cos4 | subj), where sin4 and cos4 are sinusoids with periods of π/2 (sin4 = sin(4ϕF2); cos4 = sin(4ϕF2)).
The model's joint test of the two fixed effects (cos4 and sin4) was not significant (F(2,60) = 1.0355, p = 0.3613).

The third LME model directly fit the JO17 and BR22 model predictions as the two fixed factors to test directly whether each of the computational models predicted the behaviour or the NDR as observed in CI users.

The model structure was: y ~ br22 + jo17 + (1 + br22 + jo17 | subj), where br22 contains the BR22 model predictions of the NDR amplitude as a function of relative AM starting phase, and jo17 contains the same model predictions from the JO17 model.

An ANOVA leveraging the Satterthwaite method for degrees of freedom showed a significant effect of the BR22 model (F(1,8.383) = 17.242, p = 0.0029), with no significant effect of the JO17 model (F(1,56.44) = 0.0063, p = 0.937), nor the intercept (F(1,53.421) = 0.129, p = 0.721).

Taken together, the results from these three LMEs suggest that variations in NDR amplitude with relative phase are consistent with the predictions of the BR22 model, and provide no evidence that they are consistent with those of the JO17 model.

Because refractoriness is dominant in the BR22 model while facilitation is dominant in the JO17 model, this suggests that refractoriness could be a stronger mechanistic contributor to the NDR than facilitation.

The objective of the fourth and final experiment was to assess the effect on the NDR of alternating the leading polarity of the two interleaved, AM pulse trains.

In all of the experiments reported so far the biphasic F1 and F2 pulses were always in cathodic-leading polarity, with the result that for each pulse pair the adjacent phases of the two pulses had opposite polarity.

Here we compare this "fixed polarity" stimulation to an "alternating polarity" condition where the second pulse in each pair was anodic-leading, potentially producing summation between the two central anodic phases.

Evidence for this increased facilitation or summation comes from a psychophysical experiment by Macherey et al who reported substantially lower MCLs for trains of pulse pairs where the central phases were anodic compared to when one was anodic and the other cathodic [29].

text.text: The hypothesis was that for the same stimulating current levels, the constructive betweenpulse interaction in this second 'alternating-polarity' condition would result in a larger NDR amplitude than in the control condition where both stimulating pulses had a cathodic-leading polarity.

A two-tailed t-test for the difference between NDR amplitudes (𝐴 𝐴𝑃 -𝐴 𝐹𝑃 ) across participants was not appropriate due to evidence of deviation from a normal distribution using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality test (k-stat = 0.67, critical value = 0.45, p = 0.0005).

A nonparametric Wilcoxon signed rank test on the difference between NDR amplitudes (𝐴 𝐴𝑃 -𝐴 𝐹𝑃 ) across participants was performed instead, which found a difference significantly higher than 0 dB (signed rank = 33, p = 0.0391).
This result does not survive corrections for multiple comparisons (as we also tested for phase differences) where the significance threshold is shifted to α = 2/0.025.
The average size of the difference was about 3.65 ± 3.51 dB (variation representative of 95% confidence intervals calculated without correction for multiple comparisons).
A Komogorov-Smirnov normality test did not demonstrate evidence that the phases of these responses (𝜙 𝐴𝑃 -𝜙 𝐹𝑃 ) differed from a normal distribution (k-stat = 0.38, critical value = 0.45, p = 0.15).

Therefore a standard two-tailed t-test was performed, which did not reveal a difference between the conditions (t(7) = 1.47, 95% confidence intervals = -0.93 -0.40 radians, p = 0.184), contrary to our hypothesis of a change in dominance of the underlying mechanism (from refractoriness to facilitation).

We explored mechanisms underlying the generation of neural distortions (NDRs) to stimulation with alternating-frequency, interleaved, amplitude-modulated pulse trains ("ALFIES" stimuli) in cochlear implant users.
The results provide insight into the temporal integrations at play, in addition to highlighting stimulation parameters important for optimising the SNR of NDRs.
The first experiment demonstrated that both quadratic and cubic neural-distortion responses can be observed using the ALFIES technique.
Previous work had not isolated multiple distortion products [9], [11], whereas here the F1 frequency was shifted from 80 to 82 to isolate QDRs (38 Hz) and CDRs (44 Hz) from each other.
text.formatted: Previous work had not isolated multiple distortion products <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, whereas here the F1 frequency was shifted from 80 to 82 to isolate QDRs (38 Hz) and CDRs (44 Hz) from each other.

text.text: Quadratic distortions were generally larger and more frequently observed than cubic distortions.
The observation of a relatively consistent phase difference between the QDR and CDRs (and therefore of possible cancellation between the two) inspired the second experiment.
That revealed an effect of relative AM phase between the F1-and F2-AM modulated pulse trains on the amplitude of the NDR (when QDR and CDR are constrained to the same frequency).
At the group level, the highest SNRs were observed when the maxima of the AM were aligned between the two interleaved pulse trains.

A comparison of the data to the predictions of two computational models provided evidence that refractoriness (but not facilitation) was likely responsible for the interaction between F1 and F2 pulse trains that was necessary for NDR generation.

Experiment 2 also showed that optimal selection of relative-AM phase can give rise to ALFIES NDR amplitudes comparable to those observed from eASSRs with the same stimulation parameters (within a 2.65 dB window).
The third experiment investigated interaction effects between separated distortion products and relative AM phase.
It showed that, at the group level, the NDRs when the CDR and QDR fell at the frequency were consistent with a simple sum of the two components.
However this conclusion was tempered by the small sample size and idiosyncratic effects of relative phase in some participants.
The fourth and final experiment investigated the effects of alternating the leading polarity between the F1 and F2 pulses to create a centrally effective phase.

This manipulation produced idiosyncratic effects across participants, resulting in increases ranging between 3.2 and 11.1 dB in the NDR amplitude relative to the fixed-phase condition in 4 participants, with no effect in the remaining 5; this effect did not survive correction for multiple comparisons at the group level.

The experimental and modelling results presented here indicate that refractoriness could account both for the interaction between F1 and F2 pulses and the nonlinearity that are necessary for the generation of an NDR.
If this is correct, it shows that the NDR can arise from a single process in which the temporal dependency and nonlinearity are not separate processes, as originally assumed, but intertwined.

In the context of the BR22 model, this arises from spike generation which is inherently nonlinear (incorporating rectification, as there are no 'negative spikes') on one hand, and leads to refractoriness (a temporal dependency) on the . other.
However, it is not possible to rule out alternative or additional mechanisms.

For example, at the level of the auditory nerve the effects of accommodation may be qualitatively similar to those of refractoriness, in that the response to a pulse may be reduced by the presentation of a preceding, high-amplitude pulse.

However, evidence against this explanation comes from findings that accommodation -at least in animal studies -increases with increasing inter-pulse interval up to about 500 μs, whereas the NDR is constant for IPIs between 8 and about 200-400 us, after which it decreases [11].

text.text: In addition, the fact that scalpbased EEG recordings are less sensitive to auditory-nerve and brainstem responses than to cortical responses means that we are necessarily recording the cumulative effects of multiple processing stages, any or all of which may be highly nonlinear.

What we can conclude, however, is that the temporal dependencies necessary for the NDR generation are likely present at the level of the auditory nerve, and that the spike generation and refractoriness known to operate at that level are sufficient to explain the pattern of results described here and previously.

Future experiments either with implanted recording electrodes in animals or perhaps tympanic-membrane electrodes with humans may be able to more selectively measure the effects of peripheral processes in isolation.
A second consideration is that the present results were obtained at a single pulse rate and (except for experiment 4) a single IPI of 200 μs.
It is therefore possible that the relative roles of refractoriness and facilitation would be different at either shorter or longer IPIs.
However, a re-analysis of the data reported by Guérit et al [11] revealed that the phase of the NDR was approximately constant for IPIs ranging from 8 to 948 μs (not shown here).

Both the eASSR and ALFIES have been proposed as objective measures of loudness [11], [14], [32], with the potential clinical application of informing the audiological fitting of MCLs in patients unable to make reliable subjective responses.
text.formatted: Both the eASSR and ALFIES have been proposed as objective measures of loudness <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>, with the potential clinical application of informing the audiological fitting of MCLs in patients unable to make reliable subjective responses.

text.text: For example, the eASSR has been shown to correlate with acoustic ASSRs and subjective loudness judgements in patients with a CI in one ear and normal hearing in the other [33], and the slope of the eASSR amplitude growth function correlates with the subjective dynamic range in long-term CI users [14].
text.formatted: For example, the eASSR has been shown to correlate with acoustic ASSRs and subjective loudness judgements in patients with a CI in one ear and normal hearing in the other <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>, and the slope of the eASSR amplitude growth function correlates with the subjective dynamic range in long-term CI users <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: However the eASSR requires high-rate sampling systems to isolate the neural response from the CI electrical artefacts, is limited to moderate carrier pulse rates, and produces artefacts that are larger when recorded ipsilateral compared to contralateral to the CI.
ALFIES overcomes these problems but, in previous studies, produced an NDR that had a lower amplitude than the eASSR.

The present study shows that a judicious choice of relative phase increases the NDR amplitude so as to be comparable to the eASSR, while largely avoiding the electrical artefact and allowing measurement using a technique that permits wide range of pulse rates and recording montages.
